analysis.one_liner: Restores consumers' legal rights to copy, resell, and unlock the digital music, movies, and books they buy.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced in December 2005 with bipartisan sponsorship, it got no hearing or vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The BALANCE Act would have changed federal copyright law so that people who legally buy digital music, movies, and books can use them the way they always could with physical copies: make personal backup copies, play them on any device they choose, and resell them to another person. It would also let people break the copy-protection locks on works they own when the locks stop them from a legal use, such as playing a purchased song on a competing device, if the copyright owner does not provide a way to do it themselves. The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who legally buy digital entertainment gain the right to back up, move between devices, and resell what they bought without fear of a lawsuit. Technology companies that make music players, e-readers, and other devices gain room to build interoperable products, and libraries and researchers gain clearer fair-use protections in the digital world.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers who buy digital music and movies

how_it_helps.text: It confirms that fair use — the long-standing right to quote, copy for personal use, and adapt copyrighted works — covers analog and digital transmissions alike, putting digital media on the same footing as physical media.

It makes it legal for someone who lawfully obtains a digital work to reproduce, store, adapt, or access it for archival purposes and to play it on any digital device of their choice, as long as it is not shown publicly.
It extends the 'first sale' doctrine to digital works: an owner could sell or give away a digital copy by sending it to a single recipient as long as they do not keep a usable copy themselves.

It allows a lawful owner to bypass copy-protection (DRM) technology when necessary to make a noninfringing use, if the copyright owner fails to provide a way to do that without extra cost or burden, and allows tools that do so to be built and sold.
It overrides nonnegotiable 'click-through' license terms that try to take away these consumer rights.

analysis.who_pays: Music labels, movie studios, publishers, and other large copyright holders would lose the power to charge separately for each device or format, control resale of digital works, and use DRM locks to restrict what buyers can do with purchases. They argue the changes would also make unauthorized mass copying easier.
analysis.who_pays_short: Music, movie, and publishing copyright holders

drawbacks.text: Easier circumvention of copy-protection could enable piracy: once a DRM-free copy exists, it can spread without limit, which is the core concern of copyright owners about their revenues.

The bill's test for legal circumvention — that the use is 'noninfringing' and the copyright owner failed to provide a means — would require case-by-case judgment, creating uncertainty about where the line falls.
Extending first sale to digital transfers, even with the requirement that the seller not keep a retrievable copy, is harder to verify than handing over a physical disc, raising enforcement questions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the bill would have restored rights they had with records, tapes, and DVDs — backup copies, device choice, resale — in the digital marketplace, at a real but debatable cost to copyright holders' control and revenue. The strongest honest objection is that loose DRM rules can feed piracy, though the bill tried to limit that by tying circumvention to lawful uses and requiring owners to provide alternatives first.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, so the bill died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Zoe Lofgren introduced the bill on December 14, 2005, with original cosponsors Rep. Rick Boucher and Rep. John Doolittle, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, where it remained.
The complete action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The major record labels, movie studios, and publishers are better off, because the copyright law that lets them restrict what buyers do with digital purchases through DRM locks and nonnegotiable licenses remained untouched. Consumers kept the narrower rights the DMCA left them.

for.name: Rep. Zoe Lofgren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore consumer rights to back up, transfer, and resell lawfully obtained digital works.

for.name: Rep. John Doolittle
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, making the effort bipartisan.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill's referral: no hearing, no markup, no vote, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Recording and motion picture industry lobbying groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed this family of DRM-reform bills as tools that would facilitate piracy and undercut digital sales controls.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's three sponsors split two Democrats and one Republican, but with only two cosponsors it never came to a vote, so no roll call recorded where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Music, motion picture, and publishing copyright holders
industries.note: The bill would end their ability to use DRM locks and nonnegotiable licenses to control playback devices, block resale, and charge repeatedly for the same content. Consumers would gain rights that cut into that control.

Interoperability rights and legal circumvention tools would let device and software makers build products that play any lawfully purchased media, which is what consumers want. Their interest runs with the public's here.
Explicit confirmation that fair use covers digital transmissions, plus legal archival copying, makes preservation and scholarship on digital works safer from DMCA liability.
